strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: principled uncertainty quantification for machine learning interatomic potentials, where deep ensembles are effective but computationally and memory intensive.

Proposes a practical single-model Bayesian approach that can be used both for training from scratch and for fine-tuning pretrained MLIPs, with demonstrated applicability to PaiNN and ORB v3 architectures.

Reports competitive or improved predictive accuracy and calibration in several settings, e.g., ammonia OOD force MAE 41.93±3.38 vs 48.03 for Deep Ensemble, and silica fine-tuning ECE 0.032±0.002 vs 0.247 for Deep Ensemble.
Provides algorithm pseudocode, architecture details, hyperparameters, and uses public datasets and standard UQ metrics (MSE, NLL, CRPS, ECE, Spearman correlation).
Includes an explicit equivariance analysis and honestly acknowledges that the current formulation excludes important irrep-based models such as MACE and UMA.
weaknesses: Overclaims inference efficiency: the abstract and introduction promise minimal computational overhead, but uncertainty quantification requires 100 stochastic forward passes in the silica experiment, versus 4 members for Deep Ensembles; no wall-clock, memory, or training-cost measurements are provided.

Overclaims being architecture-agnostic: the method explicitly cannot currently handle MACE and UMA due to irreducible representation dimensions, which are central to state-of-the-art equivariant MLIPs; only PaiNN and ORB v3 are evaluated.

Theoretical grounding of the ELBO is questionable: the prior in Eq. 9 is defined as N(0, p/(1-p) θ^2), depending on the variational mean θ, so the KL term is not a standard KL divergence between a fixed prior and a variational posterior; the 'Bayesian' claim and input-dependent posterior q(ω|x) are not adequately justified.

Empirical support is mixed and sometimes contradicts the claims: on the N-body EGNN task, Deep Ensemble achieves better NLL (−16.22 vs −12.52) and CRPS (0.020 vs 0.022) than BLIP; on silica at 1024 samples, BLIP gains vanish; and Spearman correlation is worse than Deep Ensemble (0.602 vs 0.676).

Experimental rigor is limited: baseline results for ammonia and silica are largely taken from Tan et al. (2023) without re-running under identical seeds; Deep Ensemble results in Table 1 have no error bars; only 4 seeds are used; no statistical significance tests or ablations on the inference network, KL weight λ, prior dropout p, or number of MC samples are reported.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL ('available at' is blank), unspecified MC sample counts for N-body and ammonia, unclear description of how the shared inference network produces layer-specific coefficients α_l and β_l, and no software/seed details.

Presentation issues remain: typos such as 'data-scarse', 'computional', and 'memebers'; some equations and implementation details are underspecified; Figure 3 caption references a PaiNN ensemble MAE of 6.58 kcal/mol/Å that is not visible on the plot; and the limitations discussion is incomplete.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: principled uncertainty quantification for machine-learned interatomic potentials, where training data is scarce, OOD configurations are common, and ensembles are expensive to train/store. The framing of the UQ need in simulation-based chemistry is sound.

The method is clean and practically appealing in principle: a drop-in, largely architecture-agnostic variational scheme that injects input-dependent weight noise via an inference network, requires storing only a single model, and admits a cheap MAP forward pass for mean predictions. The pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4) and the local-reparameterization wrapper aid reproducibility.

The fine-tuning experiment with a pretrained universal MLIP (ORB v3 on silica glass) is timely and useful. Fine-tuning with BLIP yields consistent MAE improvements over the deterministic ORB v3 across training sizes and matches/beats a 4-member deep ensemble at a fraction of the storage.

The ammonia results are suggestive: BLIP attains the lowest force MAE (41.93) among the reported baselines and the lowest ECE (0.091), with a strong Spearman correlation (0.863) between predicted variance and squared error, which is relevant for active learning.

The paper does include an ablation across MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles and reports multiple seeds for BLIP, and it honestly flags that MACE/UMA-style equivariant models are excluded in the current form.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty and unclear positioning. The core method is essentially Variational Dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) with input-dependent coefficients produced by an inference network, explicitly 'following Coscia et al. (2025)' (BARNN). The abstract and introduction present BLIP as a new 'scalable, architecture-agnostic variational Bayesian framework' without clearly delineating what is new versus adapted from prior work.

The central equivariance claim is asserted, not established. Section 3.3 claims BLIP preserves symmetry properties but no proof is provided (the 'Proofs and Derivations' appendix only contains the KL divergence and predictive-distribution derivations). Moreover, the same section excludes MACE and UMA, directly contradicting the 'architecture-agnostic' and 'seamlessly integrates with a vast family of invariant and equivariant models' claims. No experiment actually verifies that equivariance/invariance is preserved.

Several headline claims are contradicted or unsupported by the reported evidence. In the N-body equivariant setting, Deep Ensemble beats BLIP on all three metrics (MSE 0.057 vs 0.060, NLL -16.22 vs -12.52, CRPS 0.020 vs 0.022), yet the text says BLIP 'matches or exceeds Deep Ensembles'; the NLL gap is not marginal. On ammonia energy, BLIP (11.51±0.75) is within noise of Deep Ensemble (11.71), so 'best MAE' is unsupported. On silica, BLIP's Spearman correlation (0.602) is worse than Deep Ensemble's (0.676), which is glossed over as 'slightly underperform.' The 'well-calibrated' claim rests on a single ECE value (0.091) that is not obviously well-calibrated.

Baselines are weak and comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Deep Ensembles are limited to 4 members and reported with 'NA' variance; several baselines (ammonia, silica) are numbers copied from Tan et al. (2023) rather than re-run under identical conditions, so architecture-agnostic fair comparison is not established. The ensemble comparison is not compute-matched, and no statistical significance testing is performed despite large variance (e.g., forces 41.93±3.38 vs 48.03).

The practical gains are marginal and the efficiency claim is overstated. In the silica experiment all methods converge to ~1.26 MAE at 1024 samples with negligible differences, and small-N differences are often within error bars. For uncertainty quantification BLIP requires ~100 stochastic forward passes ('sample mean'), so the 'same inference cost as a deterministic model' claim only holds for the MAP variant that provides means but no uncertainty; the overhead for actual UQ is substantial.

Reproducibility gaps. The code link is truncated/missing in the manuscript ('available at' with no URL), and key details are incomplete (number of MC samples at train/test time, seed handling for borrowed baselines, exact training protocol differences from Tan et al.).

Presentation quality is poor: numerous typos ('data-scarse', 'memebers', 'computional', 'deepensembling', 'atompositions'), broken/merged equations (Eqs. 2-3 combined, an orphaned 'where' before Eq. 4), index mismatches in the appendix KL derivation (Eqs. 11-12 use ω^M_{ls} with prior indexed by l), inconsistent reference formatting, and a generic impact statement.

Related work and baselines for MLIP UQ are thin. Only Tan et al. (2023) is used as the UQ reference point; the broader recent literature on single-model and latent-space UQ for interatomic potentials is neither discussed nor compared, weakening the significance claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: principled uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, which is central to active learning and error-aware simulation. The framing and motivation are convincing.

The method is simple and practical, building on adaptive variational dropout with the local reparameterization trick, so it integrates with existing (equivariant) message-passing MLIPs and requires no architectural redesign. The code is released and datasets are public.

The empirical results are reasonably strong in places: BLIP achieves the best energy MAE (11.51 vs 11.71) and a large force MAE improvement (41.93 vs 48.03) on the OOD ammonia benchmark (Table 2), and the best force ECE (0.091 vs 0.108) (Table 3), with a high Spearman correlation (0.863, Fig. 2).

The silica fine-tuning experiment (Fig. 3b) is the most compelling result: fine-tuning a single pretrained ORB v3 with BLIP and using the single-pass MAP estimate outperforms a 4-member deep ensemble across training-set sizes, at a fraction of the storage/compute cost. This is a concrete, practically useful finding.

Reproducibility is good: hyperparameters (Table 4), optimizer/scheduler details, KL weighting, clamps, and architecture descriptions are provided, and the three datasets are publicly available with the same splits as prior work.
The paper is honest about a key limitation (MACE/UMA incompatibility) and includes an impact statement.
weaknesses: Originality is limited. The core machinery—adaptive variational dropout with input-dependent variance coefficients generated by an inference network, local reparameterization, and the Gaussian/KL formulation—is essentially the BARNN method (Coscia et al., 2025) adapted to the atomistic domain. The paper does not clearly delineate what is conceptually new versus what is a domain transfer, and the novelty claim ('we introduce BLIP') overstates the methodological contribution.

The architecture-agnostic and 'seamlessly integrates with equivariant models' claims are substantially weakened by the paper's own equivariance analysis: BLIP in its current form explicitly excludes MACE (Batatia et al., 2022) and UMA (Wood et al., 2025), which are arguably the dominant state-of-the-art equivariant MLIPs. Since the reparameterization trick is only safely applicable to layers without an irrep dimension, the method does not apply to the most important equivariant architectures, and this restriction is not reconciled with the abstract's generality claims.

The uncertainty estimates are not consistently superior to baselines. In the N-body EGNN setting, deep ensembles achieve clearly better NLL (−16.22 vs −12.52) than BLIP (Table 1), and on silica the Spearman correlation of BLIP (0.602) is worse than the deep ensemble (0.676). The claim of 'well-calibrated uncertainty' therefore holds only for some tasks, which is not adequately discussed.

The 'same inference cost as a deterministic model' claim is misleading for UQ. Obtaining uncertainties requires S stochastic forward passes (S=100 for silica), which in message-passing cost is comparable to or exceeds a 4-member ensemble at inference. The cost advantage is only realized for the MAP estimate, which does not provide uncertainty—these two regimes should be disentangled more carefully.

Baseline comparisons are partly borrowed from Tan et al. (2023) with no error bars (e.g., 'Deep Ensemble ±NA'), while BLIP is reported over only 4 seeds. This makes some comparisons (e.g., the marginal energy MAE gap of 11.51 vs 11.71) hard to interpret statistically. The choice to compare mainly against MC Dropout and deep ensembles omits more relevant variational/approximate-Bayesian baselines such as Bayes-by-Backprop, SWAG, or last-layer Laplace.

The prior is defined as N(0, (p/(1−p))θ²), i.e., it depends on the learned mean weights θ. Calling this a 'zero-mean Gaussian prior with fixed layerwise variance' is technically imprecise; a prior that scales with θ is not a fixed prior, and the implications for the ELBO/regularization are not discussed.

The scale/efficiency claims ('scalable', 'large-scale', 'high-throughput scientific workflows') are not substantiated by any genuine scaling experiment; the largest system is 699 atoms and the models are not foundation-scale, so the central scalability selling point remains aspirational.

Presentation has several errors and inconsistencies: repeated 'data-scarse' (should be 'data-scarce'), 'memebers', 'computional', 'atompositions', missing citation text after 'available at' in the introduction, and incorrect reference years (e.g., 'Blundell and Cornebise (1985)', 'Scarselli et al. (2021)' for a 2008 paper, 'Bronstein and Bruna (2016)'). These undermine polish.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: principled, single-model uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, which is central for active learning and error-aware simulations.

The method is clearly described and practically appealing: it is a drop-in, architecture-agnostic framework with minimal inference overhead (MAP inference matches deterministic cost) and only a small parameter increase (~0.1%), as quantified in Appendix E.

Empirically validated across a useful range of settings: the Coulomb N-body toy task, data-scarce/OOD ammonia, and, importantly, realistic large-scale fine-tuning of a pretrained ORB v3 model on silica (699 atoms) and MATPES with active learning.

The fine-tuning experiments contain clean ablations (w/ vs. w/o BLIP on the same architecture and split), which genuinely support the claim that BLIP fine-tuning improves force MAE and calibration while keeping deterministic inference cost.
Reproducibility is generally good: public datasets (N-body, Tan et al. ammonia/silica, MATPES), detailed hyperparameter tables, and full training/inference pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4).
The stochastic-equivariance proposition (Appendix A.3) is a nice theoretical insight, correctly identifying that the local reparameterization trick breaks equivariance for irrep-structured networks.
The limitations discussion is honest, explicitly flagging the exclusion of MACE/UMA and the source of the equivariance restriction.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core mechanism is an input-conditioned variant of Variational Dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) following Coscia et al. (2025), applied to MLIPs. The adaptive, inference-network-driven coefficients are inherited from prior work, so the contribution is largely a transfer/adaptation rather than a new method.

The 'architecture-agnostic' / 'seamlessly integrates with a vast family of (equivariant) models' claim is overstated. The paper itself admits it currently excludes MACE and UMA (the most widely used modern equivariant MLIPs) because the local reparameterization trick breaks equivariance on irreps, which materially narrows practical reach.

The headline claim of 'improved predictive accuracy' is not cleanly supported in the ammonia experiment: Table 3 compares only against UQ baselines from Tan et al. (2023) and reports no deterministic PaiNN baseline, so it cannot be established that the gain comes from BLIP rather than from the base model. The mechanism by which injected weight noise improves accuracy (a regularization effect?) is never analyzed.

Some comparisons are not statistically rigorous: in Table 1, Deep Ensemble results are reported with 'NA' error bars (single run), while BLIP is averaged over 4 seeds, making the EGNN comparison (where the ensemble 'wins') unreliable. Several other tables also use only 3-4 seeds.

The framework introduces several sensitive hyperparameters that are tuned per task (KL weight λ ranging 0.01-10, prior dropout p ranging 0.001-0.5, coefficient clamping ranges), suggesting significant per-dataset tuning and instability that complicates faithful reproduction and raises fairness concerns.

The Bayesian framing is somewhat loose: the prior is data/parameter-dependent (zero-mean Gaussian with variance p/(1-p)·θ²), i.e., effectively improper, and the input-dependent posterior over weights is a heuristic construction rather than a principled posterior approximation, which weakens the 'principled' UQ claim.

The calibration metric (ECE) and some baselines are taken directly from Tan et al. (2023) rather than re-computed under matched conditions, and the MATPES active-learning comparison shows only marginal gains for uncertainty-guided vs. random selection on forces (103.85 vs. 105.12 meV/Å), limiting the strength of that evidence.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important problem: principled uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, where deep ensembles are costly and single-model UQ is unreliable. The framing (single model, minimal inference overhead) is practically valuable.

Evaluated on a reasonable range of tasks, including fine-tuning a state-of-the-art pretrained model (ORB v3) on SiO2 and an active-learning loop on the MATPES PBE dataset, which are realistic and non-trivial benchmarks.

The equivariance analysis (Proposition 1 and Appendix A.3) attempts to formally characterize when the stochastic perturbation preserves symmetry, and correctly identifies that the local-reparameterization trick can break equivariance for irreducible representations.

The computational cost analysis (Appendix E, Table 6) makes a concrete and plausible case that BLIP adds negligible inference overhead relative to a single deterministic model and is cheaper than an N-member ensemble.

Results are broadly consistent in direction across tasks: BLIP improves force MAE and ECE in the Ammonia and SiO2 experiments, and uncertainty-guided selection outperforms random selection in the MATPES active-learning experiment.
weaknesses: Limited originality: BLIP is essentially Variational Dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) with input-dependent coefficients, closely following Coscia et al. (2025) (BARNN). The main novelty is the application to MLIPs rather than a new method; the ELBO/KL derivations are standard and the input-dependent posterior is imported from prior work.

The 'architecture-agnostic' and equivariance-preservation claims are overstated. Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3 admit that the practical local-reparameterization implementation breaks equivariance for irreps and excludes MACE and UMA, which are among the most important and widely used MLIP architectures today. This substantially narrows the claimed generality.

No ablation studies. There is no isolation of input-dependent vs. constant variational dropout coefficients, no study of the KL weight λ, the prior dropout p, or the inference-network design. It is therefore unclear whether the accuracy gains come from Bayesian UQ or simply from an added regularization/perturbation effect, which is a central unresolved question.

Several reported uncertainty metrics are actually worse than baselines but are presented as strengths. In Table 2, BLIP's Spearman correlation (0.863) is below the Gaussian Mixture Model (0.904); in the SiO2 experiment, BLIP's Spearman correlation (0.602) is below Deep Ensemble (0.676). The text glosses over these losses and still describes the correlations as 'strong/reliable'.

Comparison fairness is questionable. Baseline numbers in Tables 2-3 are taken directly from Tan et al. (2023) rather than re-run under the same protocol, and the Deep Ensemble row in Table 1 reports 'NA' standard deviations (apparently a single run), so the stated error bars are not on equal footing. The claim that BLIP 'matches or exceeds Deep Ensembles' is not well supported when BLIP loses to the ensemble on EGNN.

Inconsistency in the SiO2 figure/caption: the caption states the best baseline (Deep Ensemble PaiNN) achieves MAE 6.58 kcal/mol/Å, while the plotted forces MAE values are ~1.3 kcal/mol/Å, and the comparison pits a fine-tuned pretrained ORB v3 against a from-scratch PaiNN ensemble, which is not apples-to-apples.

Reproducibility is weak. No code or artifact release is mentioned, and the method requires task-specific tuning (e.g., clamping VAD coefficients to [1e-5, 0.11], prior p=0.01, λ=0.001 for ORB v3), which the authors justify by claiming the pretrained weights are 'highly sensitive to even minimal perturbations'—raising the concern that results depend on delicate hyperparameter choices.

Overstated claims: 'well-calibrated' and 'improved predictive accuracy' margins are often modest and sometimes within reported noise (e.g., Ammonia energy 11.51±0.75 vs 11.71). Additionally, the epistemic/aleatoric decomposition of Eq. (14) is presented but never actually computed or evaluated, so it contributes nothing.
The N-body experiment is a toy particle-position task (not energy/force prediction) that is only loosely connected to the paper's MLIP focus and does not strengthen the core claims.

Presentation issues: the reference list contains numerous citation-year mismatches (e.g., 'Kulichenko et al. (2017)' for a 2024 paper, 'Scarselli et al. (2017)' for 2008, 'Kaplan et al. (2014)' for 2025), indicating a lack of care in the manuscript.

strengths: Targets an important and practical problem: reliable uncertainty quantification for MLIPs in data-scarce, out-of-distribution, and active-learning settings.

Proposes a scalable variational Bayesian framework built on adaptive variational dropout with input-dependent coefficients, local reparameterization, and a single trained model; MAP inference adds no inference overhead and training is about 1.9x base cost.
Empirically validates BLIP on four diverse tasks (Coulomb N-body, OOD NH3, 699-atom SiO2 fine-tuning of ORB v3, MATPES active learning) with multiple metrics (MSE, NLL, CRPS, MAE, ECE, Spearman).

Demonstrates improved accuracy and calibration in several settings: e.g., NH3 forces MAE 41.93 vs 48.03 for Deep Ensembles and ECE 0.091 vs 0.108; SiO2 ECE 0.032 vs 0.247; MATPES energy MAE 91.13 vs 96.65 for BLIP+random and 111.83 without BLIP.
Provides a useful efficiency analysis showing BLIP requires roughly 0.1-5% extra parameters, MAP inference matches deterministic inference cost, and avoids N-times ensemble storage and computation.

Includes an equivariance analysis with a proposition for stochastic equivariant maps and an honest discussion that the local reparameterization trick currently breaks equivariance for irreps, excluding MACE/UMA in the current implementation.
Reproducibility is supported by public datasets, detailed hyperparameters, training algorithms, and compute setup.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with helpful figures and tables.
weaknesses: The central novelty—input-dependent adaptive variational dropout—is not isolated: there is no ablation against standard input-independent variational dropout or fixed-coefficient Bayesian training, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from adaptivity versus stochastic regularization.

The 'architecture-agnostic' claim is overstated: the current local-reparameterization implementation excludes important state-of-the-art equivariant MLIPs such as MACE and UMA because it breaks equivariance for irreducible representations; only GNN, EGNN, PaiNN, and ORB v3 are tested.

Several comparisons are statistically weak: Deep Ensembles in the N-body experiment have ±NA, NH3 baselines from Tan et al. are single numbers without standard deviations, and no Deep Ensemble active-learning baseline is reported on MATPES; some improvements (e.g., NH3 energy 11.51±0.75 vs 11.71) are within noise.

Method specification and reproducibility are partially ambiguous: the inference network's output dimension ('head-dim') and the exact mapping of α/β to weights/activations (per-layer, per-neuron, or per-weight) are not clearly defined, and no code release is mentioned.
The KL derivation in Appendix A.1 appears to omit a factor of 1/2 relative to the standard Gaussian KL, yielding twice the standard KL; even if absorbed by λ, the derivation as written is incorrect.

The Bayesian formulation is nonstandard: the variational posterior is conditioned on the input, the ELBO uses MAE + KL rather than an explicit likelihood for energy/force targets, and no aleatoric variance term is learned, so calibration claims are largely empirical rather than theoretically grounded.

No sensitivity analyses are provided for key hyperparameters (KL weight λ, prior dropout p, coefficient clamping, inference-network size, number of MC samples), despite these being set differently per task (e.g., λ=10 for NH3 vs 0.001 for silica).

The paper lacks comparisons to other Bayesian/UQ methods (e.g., Bayes by Backprop, SWAG, Laplace approximation) and does not compare BLIP-based active learning against ensemble-based uncertainty selection, which would strengthen the UQ claims.
In the silica experiment, BLIP has worse uncertainty-error rank correlation than Deep Ensembles (Spearman 0.602 vs 0.676), so the 'trustworthy uncertainty' claim is nuanced despite better ECE.
There is no discussion of broader ethical or societal implications, though this is a minor point for a methods paper.
